newsitem.title: USA: Niche essential for professional practices, too.
newsitem.headline: Niche essential for professional practices, too.

text.p: A special market niche is just as essential for the professional practitioner hanging out a shingle for the first time as it is for anyone launching a new business.
Even if one succeeds in developing a speciality that results in a successful niche, as in any business, it requires a continuous effort to make that niche known to potential clients.

For example, Ira Levine, a Great Neck, N.Y., accountant, worked over a 14-year period for three of the largest firms in the tiny field of royalty compliance management. The first case he worked on involved a 1917 recording contract between the Victor Talking Machine Company, precursor to RCA, and a young Jascha Heifetz, whose father had to sign the document for the prodigy violinist.
Another case early in Levine's career involved Michael Jackson, who had released a single album, Off the Wall.
"Doing it all those years, I knew I could do this on my own, without an organisation behind me," said Levine. "I knew that if I could get the work, I could organise doing the job."

A year ago, Levine, 39, decided he was tired of spending so much time on the road, away from his wife and three young children. With his wife, Sandra Domnitz, a former sales and marketing manager, they decided to set up their own company.

The service is valuable to anyone receiving royalties, not necessarily because someone is dishonest, but rather because all contracts are open to interpretation. "A contract is always open to at least two points of view," said Levine.

His particular area of accounting is not well known, even among those firms and individuals who could benefit from it. But it's often beneficial for musicians, inventors, artists, sports figures and others with special claims to a song, logo, signature or another licensed product the produces royalty income.

"The previous work revolved around the agreement in effect that the artist had with the company -- the publisher, the record company, the studio. They would receive regular royalty payments based on the terms of the contract and the sales or usage of a product, or the exposure, if it could be measured some way," said Levine.

"I represent the party that receives the compensation. On his behalf, I examine the books and determine whether he should have received more," he said. "Maybe he's getting just a nickel instead of six cents.
"It's funny how whenever there are discrepancies, it's usually against my client. I'm not insinuating that they might be intentional, but that's the way it happens."
They converted the top floor of their home into an office, invested in an 800- number, two additional phone lines and a fax machine and launched their company, called Compensation Management.

"When I left my employer, I had an understanding not to do business with existing clients for two years. So I was going to go into a different field, knowing that the type of work would be similar for anyone who has a compliance agreement. So I focused on merchandise licensing agreements. That's royalties on sales of T-shirts, mugs, etc."

Checking out industry associations for merchandisers, they bought a source-list from a firm that lists licensees, lincensors, agents, products and other details on those involved in selling licensed merchandise. Domnitz hired an all-day baby-sitter to care for the children and started calling 50 to 100 companies daily from the list.

"When I started doing this, I didn't know what I was talking about," she confessed. "But Ira had tremendous confidence in my sales ability. I was talking about what we could do for other people, but I was just a page ahead of who I was talking to in terms of knowing what licensing is about."

But she was savvy enough to realise two key points -- "That these people don't perform a lot of audits, or they would have seen my areas of weakness, and that when there is a need, people respond to it. The service actually sold itself."

She also realised that there were very few people offering Levine's speciality. "If Ira was selling himself just as a CPA, it wouldn't help. There are many many CPAs. It's essential to establish a niche field."
The Atlanta Olympics Committee was one of the first potential clients she called last February, following up with a brochure and a separate letter. But it wasn't until May that they landed a deal.

The Committee had the rights to the torch symbol, which was the symbol for the Atlanta games. Licenses were granted to 160 companies to use the symbol on their products, with a royalty from each going to the Committee.

"Before we start a job we review agreements and correspondence, and based on that review, we determine whether it warrants an examination," said Levine. "Sometimes the potential findings are small, or sometimes there are certain restrictions or limitations because of contract language, so you wouldn't perform an examination.
Payment is based either on an hourly fee or a percentage of recovery.

"Recognizing that fees probably run in the neighbourhood of $5,000 for a week, an examination might include a few days doing field work, looking at the records and then followup and preparing a report, so a job might take one to two weeks," Levin said. "At that point, we will see whether there's reason to continue. If we recognise there won't be recovery, we stop right there to be fair with the client. But it's almost always cost-beneficial."
